R_H1.passageTitle: How Impersonation Scams Changed Their Route

passages.label: A
passages.text: A message that appears to come from a legitimate business can still be deceptive, and a hostile tone or a disturbing claim about a frozen account can make a person feel that they must act before they have time to check. A malicious sender may use a fabricated account notice to present a fraudulent payment as the only way to resolve the problem. Financial loss can have devastating consequences, and the first step when you run into this kind of message is to check how you know who sent it.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The route changed sharply between 2020 and 2023. Reports beginning with a phone call fell, while those beginning with an email or text increased, and a deceptive message may warn of suspicious account activity or an unauthorised purchase, and it provides a number or asks for a short reply. The person who answers pretends to solve the invented problem, but the solution moves the victim's money. Reports also show chains of impersonation, and a fake company employee may transfer a caller to a fake bank worker and then to someone claiming to represent an agency, and each role makes the story appear more official. The volume of complaints reflects both offending and reporting behaviour, so a rapid increase can identify an emerging method without establishing its prevalence. Investigators use independent verification to separate reports about suspected deception from records of confirmed transactions.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Other scripts create a different kind of pressure, and a phony subscription notice claims that an unfamiliar service will renew for hundreds of dollars. If the recipient calls, the scammer requests remote access and creates the appearance of an excessive refund, and the victim is told to return the difference with gift cards. In another script, a fake government agent says that the victim's identity is connected with a serious crime. Cash placed in a Bitcoin ATM is described as being kept in a safety locker. Delivery messages use realistic logos, request a small redelivery fee and then capture card details, and a separate fake giveaway promises a prize only after money is sent.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Categorising complaints gives law enforcement insight into the demographic groups offenders target. Identity theft can affect a person’s livelihood, and even a law-abiding retailer can be impersonated, and a person can take steps to verify a claim by contacting the real business offline. Authorities may then trace patterns in reported payments to help combat crime, and a report can inform work on public safety even when investigators still need separate evidence to confirm what happened in that case. Earlier FTC analysis classified recurring narratives from 850 detailed reports. The most common five categories accounted for nearly half of relevant 2023 reports, suggesting recurring impersonation patterns without estimating their prevalence across different demographic groups in the wider population.

passages.label: E
passages.text: The FTC advises recipients to verify the claim through a channel they find independently, and a report can help agencies combat impersonation and hold people accountable across related cases. Keep the original message so investigators can assemble and compare records. Companies that regulate activity on their own networks can act on accounts used to impersonate others. Confronting the request calmly allows time for verification and limits the negative consequences of a rushed decision, particularly where someone demands an irreversible transfer or disclosure of sensitive account information.

passages.label: A
passages.text: The FBI created its Internet Crime Complaint Center, or IC3, in May 2000, and people who run into suspected fraud can report what happened, including requests that exhibit signs of deception. A disturbing claim from a sender may turn out to be part of a real dispute, and a legitimate payment can be mistaken for a fraudulent one. Investigators need information that helps distinguish the two. By 2024 the centre had logged more than nine million complaints since it began.

passages.label: B
passages.text: An individual complaint may allege identity theft or describe a potential interruption to a victim’s livelihood. Comparing many complaints gives law enforcement more insight into whom offenders target and when people report losses, and a retailer may provide records to help officers trace funds. An investigation must respect protections for law-abiding people, including judicial authorisation of a warrant where required. To combat crime, public agencies can take steps to pass warnings and verified information on to the groups responsible for public safety. Phishing and spoofing accounted for the highest volume of complaints, 193,407, whereas investment fraud produced the greatest aggregate loss, approximately 6.57 billion dollars. Complaint frequency and aggregate monetary losses require distinct indicators.

passages.label: C
passages.text: IC3 established its Recovery Asset Team in 2018 to coordinate financial institutions and FBI field offices, including requests to freeze funds sent in fraudulent transactions in the United States or abroad through the Financial Fraud Kill Chain. Business email compromise accounts for most requests, although the process can assist in other cases involving fraudulent transfers. Requests in 2024 covered 3,020 complaints and 848.4 million dollars in attempted theft. The 469.1 million dollars frozen in domestic cases and the 92.5 million frozen internationally yielded a reported combined success rate of 66 per cent.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Speed can change an outcome. In one 2024 property case, buyers received a deceptive email that appeared to come from their real-estate agents and wired 956,342 dollars. They recognised the false instructions two days later. After IC3 was notified, the Recovery Asset Team acted and 955,060 dollars was returned. In another case, a request from Singapore concerned a transfer of approximately 6.66 million dollars, and a United States bank froze 5.1 million, while efforts continued to trace money sent onward to Spain and China. These examples show why victims should report promptly rather than wait for a private investigation to finish.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Analysts can assemble in teams to compare individual complaints with other information, and the combined data can connect cases, track threats, support public warnings and guide referrals to law enforcement. Operation Level Up used complaint data to identify people caught in cryptocurrency investment fraud. In 2024, 4,323 victims were notified, and 76 per cent did not yet know they were being scammed. The operation estimated savings of more than 285 million dollars. Forty-two people were referred for suicide intervention. Strong reporting cannot eliminate cybercrime, but it can help agencies combat it, prosecute offenders and make platforms more accountable, and the figures can guide efforts to regulate risky activity. For victims, fast action may prevent a devastating loss rather than merely document it later, and a temporary hold can limit a loss while agencies confront the larger pattern. It does not resolve the question of who was responsible. The available complaint figures describe suspected incidents, whereas a prosecution depends on corroborated evidence and a separate legal process.

passages.label: A
passages.text: Traditional security advice often focuses on the user, and people are told to create stronger passwords, install updates and recognise suspicious messages. CISA's Secure by Design programme asks a different question: why was the product unsafe when it reached the customer? Guidance issued with international partners argues that the burden should not fall only on users and small technology teams. Manufacturers should take ownership of the security outcomes connected with their products, and the approach does not excuse users from sensible behaviour. It changes where prevention begins, asking companies to confront avoidable weaknesses during design and development instead of treating every failure as a customer mistake.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The guidance sets out three principles. First, manufacturers should own customer security outcomes and invest in safer architecture, features and default settings. Second, they should practise radical transparency and remain accountable when weaknesses appear. Complete vulnerability notices and accurate public records help customers respond and allow the industry to learn. Third, leaders should treat security as a business priority. Executives are expected to create incentives and structures that support secure development. Technical teams cannot eliminate recurring defects if senior decisions reward only speed or low cost. Leadership must give product security the same sustained attention as other business goals.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Secure by Default turns those principles into the normal starting condition. Important controls should already be enabled, and customers should not pay extra for basic protection. CISA compares this expectation with seatbelts supplied in new cars. Products should avoid universal default passwords, support strong multifactor authentication and provide useful security logs, and a secure setting should not require an overloaded administrator to discover a complicated option. These practices help organisations combat attacks before a malicious actor finds an easy route, and they also reduce the need for repeated warnings that ask millions of users to compensate for one weak product design.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The 2024 pledge encouraged manufacturers to take steps that customers can evaluate. An update may strengthen encryption or establish a default connection to a secure network without individual configuration. There is still a trade-off when a company decides how much information to record. Diagnostic records give insight into how teams trace problems and assess exposure to identity theft. A supplier can explain how the design considers public safety. Product improvements and investigations by law enforcement support different ways to combat crime. As a voluntary commitment directed to enterprise software manufacturers, the pledge asks participants to publish evidence of progress within a year or account for the challenges they encountered. That distinction helps readers separate implementation from independent verification of outcomes. Comparable documentation can show whether a change was sustained across releases and evaluated consistently.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Later CISA and FBI guidance asked technology leaders to review earlier defects and try to eliminate recurring classes of harm. A team can assemble reports of deceptive or fraudulent messages that resemble legitimate notices, and estimate how a hostile actor might use weak product defaults. That helps distinguish a disturbing report from a vulnerability with a potentially devastating effect. Product teams can make recurrence less likely while support staff resolve particular incidents. Government agencies may regulate an industry, and law enforcement may prosecute a person responsible for malicious activity. These separate responsibilities confront the same harm at different stages.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could advice about careful use coexist with the manufacturer's role described in the passage?
options: Adjust every product only after users have taken all available precautions.
Users can act sensibly while companies address avoidable problems before delivery.
A product maker can treat every problem as a mistake by a customer.
Making a product safer means every user can ignore all updates or suspicious messages.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A company promises safer design but will ship its product with basic controls switched off. Which pair of changes would reflect both the programme's leadership role and its expectations for the delivered product?
options: Offer better user instructions but let both the settings and management priorities remain unchanged.
Make safety optional and use the money received after launch to consider basic controls.
Enable the controls for internal trials but make customers add them without management support.
Have leaders support sustained safer development and enable basic controls before delivery.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How could a company undermine the principles even if it employed technical specialists?
options: Rewarding only speed or low cost could leave technical teams unable to stop recurring problems.
Making time to check product outcomes necessarily creates more defects.
Business leaders can avoid any effect on how a technical team does its work.
Clear public records make sustained leadership unnecessary.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why are security controls compared to seatbelts in new cars?
options: Safety becomes a separate service that can be bought only later.
A manufacturer can assume everyone will add it at home.
Some protection should be provided with the product itself without a special request.
A product is safe as long as an instruction names something that could protect it.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How does publishing information under the pledge relate to the earlier call for transparency?
options: A company's announcement automatically verifies every claim independently.
Transparency ends when the first update is released.
The pledge removes the need to give customers any information about weaknesses.
Publishing what changed or what remains difficult supports transparency, while independent checking is a separate issue.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What could a company examine to tell whether a change was carried forward over several versions?
options: Use comparable records over time to see whether the change remained and was assessed consistently.
Count publicity for the first version and assume every later product behaves identically.
Let the name of the pledge settle all questions about what changed.
Check only whether the company still employs the same people.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which example separates the work of preventing a repeated problem and dealing with a particular incident?
options: The same incident must be solved repeatedly before a design team can act.
Support staff alone own all decisions about which industry laws apply.
One team can change a product to reduce recurrence, while other staff help with the case that already happened.
An individual report determines every other organisation's responsibilities.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A company joins the pledge and announces one improvement. Which comparison would give a fuller account of its role?
options: Being listed as participating proves that each recurring weakness is now eliminated.
Look for sustained changes and whether leadership supports preventing similar harm, as well as what the announcement reports.
Joining the pledge proves every other company uses the same setting.
Compare only the format of the first announcement with a notice from a government agency.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What distinction does looking at both a product change and a legal response make clear?
options: Designers can reduce recurring risks, while authorities can address wrongdoing through a different process.
A product change by itself establishes exactly who committed a crime.
Prosecuting an offender directly gives every product new security controls.
A regulation removes the need for increasing safety in the products themselves.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which view fits how the article assigns responsibility from design to later responses?
options: The same safety measures can be left until every customer makes a complaint.
Responsibility belongs only to the individual user and is unchanged before delivery.
A voluntary pledge makes reporting and evidence unnecessary for any company.
Manufacturers can lead on preventing avoidable harm, make their progress open to review and work alongside those responding to individual incidents.
